rationale: The book's identification of 'the name' with 'the covenant itself' rests on a local word-substitution in 2 Sam 7 that does not establish lexical or symbolic identity across the corpus; the mainstream reading that the name stands for the person (character, presence, authority) accounts for the same texts with fewer unsupported equivalences, covers the self-revelation and exaltation passages more directly, and still explains the relational, marital, and fidelity themes without redefining the referent. The marriage and wing imagery are real but function as belonging/ownership under the person, not as proof that the name equals the covenant structure.
book_core_identification: The name is the covenant itself (the binding relationship between God and his people).
book_secondary_elaborations: Taken exactly as a bride takes her husband's name
To be called by his name is to be brought under his wing
The wing-corners carry the tassels that remind of the commandments
Asking or acting 'in the name' means inside the covenant bond rather than appending a formula
Taking the name in vain means emptying the covenant by unfaithful living
The self-made name of Babel is the opposite of the God-given covenantal name
strongest_counter_interpretation: A 'name' symbolizes the essential character, nature, identity, presence and authority of the person who bears it; God's name therefore stands for God himself, so that to know, call on, hallow, profane or act in the name is to deal with the person.
counter_core_identification: The name represents the person (character, nature, presence and authority).
material_core_denial: That 'the name' is identical with the covenant rather than with the person of God/Christ whose character and authority the covenant expresses.
counter_case: Exodus 3:13-15 and 34:5-7 present the divine name as ontological and moral self-disclosure of God's being and character, not as a covenant instrument.
Standard 'name theology' (Deut 12; 1 Kgs 8; 2 Sam 7:13) uses 'house for my name' for the place of divine presence; the ark is associated but not equated with the name.
Prayer, healing, baptism and salvation 'in the name' (John 14:13-14; Acts 3:6; 4:12; Matt 28:19) consistently mean by the authority or person of Jesus, not by a covenant entity.
Philippians 2:9-11 and the 'name above every name' language result in personal worship of Jesus, not of a covenant.
Knowing, trusting or calling on the name (Ps 9:10; Prov 18:10; Joel 2:32/Rom 10:13) is treated as relating directly to the LORD himself.

The 'Lord, Lord' rejection (Matt 7) and 'take the name in vain' (Ex 20:7) are explained by acting inconsistently with the person's character and authority without requiring that the name be redefined as the covenant.
book_explanatory_advantages: Tightly links Isa 4:1 and Ruth 3:9 marital 'called by thy name' / wing imagery to covenant ownership.
Gives a coherent non-magical account of unanswered 'in Jesus' name' prayers and of the lawless who still use the name.
Unifies name-bearing, law-keeping and the Lord's Prayer petitions under one relational theme.
Explains profanation of the name by unfaithful living (Ezek 36) without reducing it to speech alone.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Covers the full range of name usages (self-revelation, presence, authority, reputation, new identity) with a single, non-reductive referent—the person—without forcing every text through a covenant equation.
Fits Exodus 3 and Philippians 2 without residual contradiction or redefinition.
Matches the broad, multi-tradition consensus and the ordinary grammatical force of 'in the name of X'.
Still accommodates the marital and fidelity texts as expressions of belonging to the person rather than as proofs that the name equals the covenant.
Requires fewer interpretive leaps than equating the 2 Sam 7 substitution with ontological identity of name and covenant.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Exodus 3:14 'I AM WHO I AM' as disclosure of eternal self-existence; reducing this to 'the covenant' collapses ontology into relationship and contradicts the text's emphasis on being.

Acts 4:12 (and the surrounding healing narrative in Acts 3–4) presents salvation by 'the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth' as the person who healed the lame man; treating the name as the covenant severs the name from the concrete agent of the miracle.

Philippians 2:9-11 bestowal of 'the name that is above every name' so that every knee bows to Jesus is personal exaltation and worship; a covenant cannot be the direct object of that universal homage without contradiction.
decisive_sources: 2 Samuel 7:13 read against the broader Deuteronomic name-theology corpus
unresolved_objections: The book's non-formulaic reading of 'in my name' and its emphasis on life-consistency remain valuable correctives even if the core identification fails.
The marital and wing imagery is genuinely present and under-appreciated in some popular treatments, though it does not compel equating name with covenant.
